utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I believe that the Chamber had been informed through the legal officer that the witness whom we were examining at the end of -- well, before we rose on Friday, the 9th of November, has unfortunately had to return to Bosanski Samac because of a death in the family. It was the father-in-law, who was sick prior to him giving testimony, but that testimony was given on short notice because of the shortened time of cross-examination of Sulejman Tihic. In the intervening period, the father-in-law has died and the witness has had to return home to look after the funeral arrangements and that. He will be available towards the end of the week for cross, but we propose that we would then move straight ahead and call the next witness, who is a protected witness, subject to a prior order from 1999, and has been given the pseudonym Witness G. And Defence counsel were advised of the situation once the Prosecution learned what had happened to the witness, Mr. Dagovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Witness G has also got facial distortion, face distortion?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Witness G has facial distortion, and I believe she has also requested voice distortion. I'm not sure whether that has been put in place this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the order did say that the witness has got a pseudonym and face distortion, and, upon request, can be granted voice distortion, and that has been put in place, we've been told.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is happy to proceed as the order has indicated, facial distortion and voice distortion, because the witness would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the voice distortion, both parties, when asking the witness -- after the question, you switch off the microphone, otherwise the voice of the witness will go through your system and then can be heard outside. So it's a bit of a mechanical aspect. I want to hear from the Defence. Have you been informed about the change of witness? We can't have the other witness for cross-examination this morning, as stated by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, indeed we have been advised by the OTP that this unfortunate thing has happened with Mr. Esad Dagovic and that they would like to proceed with Witness G, and we don't have any objection to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to remind -- to ask the Prosecution: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [redacted] Now, the Trial Chamber would like to know whether this is still on or it has been -- it has fallen through, because throughout, the Prosecution -- his name was being mentioned. So can we have a submission on that? What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour is correct. That witness's name has actually been put on the public record. And the reason for the initial protective measures was because Witness A had -- whilst in detention had been subjected to treatment -- it was, in particular, of a sexual nature, and it was a request for a matter of privacy, personal privacy. Whilst that person's name has been put on the record as of him being a person detained and a victim of beatings, so far his name has not come up with specific incidents of that nature, and for that reason, if the witness is still to testify, we would ask that, when testifying, he be protected so that he would not be identified as a specific victim of that treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll come to that when he actually comes --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- and can testify. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Of course, we have also -- although the name has been put on the record, I've sought to ensure that his name would never be directly linked with either the pseudonym or with that treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we can go ahead. The witness can be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just before the witness is called, may I just seek a procedural clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: It concerns how Your Honour would like to proceed with the witness identification. I have a sheet of paper which I have left with the Registry and with the Defence, indicating the witness's name, date of birth and place of birth, which I could propose to put to the witness and to have the witness confirm whether or not those are indeed the details, and then those persons in the courtroom could also confirm that we are indeed dealing with the appropriate pseudonym. After that, as has been practiced, there would be a couple of biographical questions I would like to put to her about where she came from and connections with the area she used to live in, and that might, of course, lead to identification of the witness, and I would request, if it's possible, that this first few minutes just be done in private session so that there's no identifying information, and I believe the Defence counsel wouldn't have an objection to that. I did run it by them this morning and I think that they feel that that's satisfactory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Normally that's what we do. We use a piece of paper where the particulars are printed, and then the piece of paper is admitted into evidence under seal, and it will have a number. So that's normally the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I do hope that the Defence have no objection to going into private session for the first few questions, as indicated by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We don't have any objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can proceed. We'll go into private session after the solemn declaration and after the piece of paper --

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Please make your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Reidy:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think I've already explained to you that you are -- you have certain measures which are protecting your identity whilst you give your testimony to the Chamber, and for that reason, I'm not going to ask you to put your name on the record. However, you will now be shown a piece of paper, and when you're shown the piece of paper, I'd like you to confirm whether or not the details on that paper refer to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the registry to present the witness with the piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just confirm for me at the letter "A", that's your name, is it? That is your name at the letter "A", is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is your date of birth at letter "B"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the letter "C", is that the place where you were born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: And I'd ask the Chamber now if that could be placed under seal or would the Chamber like to inspect the paper that the -- that the witness has just read out or has just read to herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The number is P34, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The Prosecution can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And at this stage, I request that that we go into private session while I ask the witness a few biographical details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are now in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, I'd like to ask you about some of the other people who were living in Bosanski Samac in April 1992. Can I ask you whether or not you know a person called Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that you knew Blagoje Simic quite well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, I knew Doctor -- Mr. Blagoje Simic when he was a boy, when he was ten years old, because I used to work with [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [redacted], so I would see him around. We didn't have a personal relationship, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I ask: Would you be able to tell me whether Blagoje Simic is sitting in this room today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: The gentleman, can I show, point him out with my hand or should I say it? The gentleman in the dark suit with the beard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the description is clear, but you can also point to him if you wish so that we all know exactly who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: The last row, where the police officer is, and then right next to him, that's the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: I think the record can show that the witness has correctly identified Mr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, but I have information from my clients that the translation into B/C/S is not heard on some of the channels, so we're not able to hear what the witness is saying in their headphones. I can hear the witness, but the accused are saying that in some changes, they're not able to follow what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Usually when we have voice distortion we normally have such problems. So I think they have to change the channel each time the witness speaks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can hear it very well on channel 7, because before it was set on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Maybe we can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was just a technical problem. So I was going to ask you about a second person who you may know from Bosanski Samac. Do you know someone called Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, how would you say -- how do you know Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I know Milan quite well. We worked together. [redacted] [redacted], and our families have had very close ties for years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could I ask you the same question? If you see Mr. Milan Simic in the room today, could you tell us and describe to us where you see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: The gentleman in the black and white shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the record could reflect that the witness has correctly identified Mr. Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone by the name of Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I just know him slightly. [redacted]. I would pass by his house and we would just greet one another: Good day, good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if he was in the courtroom today, would you be able to point us to him? Would you be able to tell us where he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman in the grey suit, with a white moustache, sitting right there.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And again, if the record could reflect that Mr. Miroslav Tadic has been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, I believe you also know Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say you knew him fairly well or very well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I think I know him very well. We were friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. We grew up together. We're friends. I am very fond of Mr. Zaric's son, Mirel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for the record, could you please indicate to the Chamber if you can see Mr. Zaric here this morning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, I see him. In the glasses. The gentleman sitting next to Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, I think the record can identify that all four defendants have been identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you just about April 1992 and events in Bosanski Samac. Can you hear me correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I just -- I positioned my headphones properly now. Yes, yes, I can hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of April 1992, did you notice any change in atmosphere in Bosanski Samac or any --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Just one moment. Yes. Yes, you could notice it. In the building where I lived, for example - and this is one thing that you could notice - very few of us would stay there over the weekend, on Saturday and Sunday. Perhaps out of the 24 residents who lived there, perhaps two or three families would stay at home. All the others would go to their families in the countryside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it this was a new development; it wasn't something that had normally happened in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was something new. Then there were some guards, and then on the 11th of April - I think it was the 11th of April - there was a meeting, a rally in the town, where people requested that some soldiers who were around be removed. They were positioned around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you attend this rally on the 11th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that it was requested that some of the soldiers who were around the town be removed. Were the soldiers removed after the rally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't know whether that happened after the rally. All I know is that Ibrahim Salkic, a fellow citizen, came out to the podium. He stood at the microphone and he addressed Mr. Simo Zaric. He asked him directly that these soldiers be removed. And Mr. Zaric then said that nobody will enter Samac, that the 4th Detachment would defend Samac from Serbs and Croats, from everybody, so this 4th Detachment will be there to save Samac from anybody who would try to move in. That's what I remember. And this person, Salkic, then said that his children were there, and he asked, "And where are their children?" And then when he said "their," he probably meant all the officials there, because many of them sent their children away. Some had sent them to Croatia, some away to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- before the 17th of April, did you ever get any other indication or warning that something was about to happen in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. There were stories going around even in our bank. Our director said one day -- since we have large windows, the bank has a lot of glass, the building, so she said that we should put tape on the windows in case there were any bomb blasts or detonations; we should put this tape on the glass so that the glass wouldn't shatter. Sometime, I think perhaps it was the 14th of April, my childhood friend, Predrag Blagojevic, came to my office and said that he had just talked to his father and that his father had told him that he was perhaps either at Obudovac or Batusa and that Arkan's men had arrived. And he said, "I'm taking my children to Novi Sad. [redacted], why don't you come with me?" My friend, my colleague, was also there, Mara Mokric, and we laughed at that and told him, "Oh, come on." His wife's name is Biljana and his mother's name is Zora. And so we were just joking, "You just want to get rid of Zora and Biljana." We thought it was some kind of joke. However, Pero left, and then three days later what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we move to those -- to that three days later? On the evening of the 16th of April, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: It was [redacted] that day, the 16th of April. Until 3.00, in the afternoon, I was at work. We were issuing paycheques. And then on that day I also sent the paycheque for Mr. Milan Simic. I sent it with Nijaz Huskic, who worked at that company as financial director. Because I hadn't seen Milan at work from Monday that week. He didn't pick up his paycheque. So I asked this man, Nijaz Huskic, "Perhaps you'll see Milan this afternoon so you can take him his salary." After 3.00, we went to a restaurant to celebrate [redacted]: Gordana Nogic, Mina Nogic, Vesna Ivkovic, Mrs. Fatima Zaric, Ruzica Markovic. We were at the restaurant until about 5.00. Then Fatima went to the shop. She had her own shop. Ruzica also left, and those who remained were Vera Ivkovic, Cica. She left as well. Gordana Nogic and Mina Nogic and myself stayed on at this restaurant, this fish restaurant. Around 7.15, 7.30, the waiter told us that they are closing and that we should leave. We went outside to the street. [redacted] [redacted], and we were planning to continue [redacted] with my brothers, at my mother's house. And you could see on the street that something was happening. We went to my mother's house, and after about five or ten minutes, Mrs. Cvijeta Bradasevic came - she is Mr. [as interpreted] Gordana Nogic's sister - and she called her to go outside. And she probably warned her that there was something wrong, that something was about to happen, because Gordana came in and said, "Oh, dear. There'll be -- war might break out." And she called her husband, Dr. Mesud Nogic, who was at a restaurant called Scorpion, to check with him what the situation was. And the answer that she got from him was, "Just keep on with your -- continue with your celebration. Nothing will happen. I've just been with Sulejman Tihic, who has just come back from Kruskovo Polje or some other place. There won't be any war. Nothing will happen. You just continue with your party." That day, my brother was completing the first cement block. He had started to build a business facility for his own son. And Mr. Djordjic Zika, called Srbin, he was the contractor who was carrying out the work, and he was the brother-in-law or the son-in-law of Milan Jovanovic. I can't remember. Gordana and Mina left at about 9.30, and we continued with our party. We stayed there. And then we received a telephone call from Milan Jovanovic. He called his son-in-law and he wanted him to come home right away. But this young man didn't go home right away, so there was another phone call. So that this young man got up and left together with this -- this Srbin, this craftsman. And then we went to bed at about 10.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you'd gone to bed. You didn't think of leaving -- you and your brothers didn't think of leaving Bosanski Samac that night, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened later that night after you'd gone to bed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. When war would be mentioned or that something would happen, I always thought about it. I don't owe anybody anything. I haven't done anything bad to anyone. Whoever wants to take power might as well. I don't want power. Nobody's going to do me any harm. So now I'll proceed along the lines of what you asked me about. We went to bed, and sometime before dawn, occasional gunfire would be heard, occasional gunfire. About 6.00 in the morning, Zijad Huskic, nicknamed Cicko, knocked at my mother's door, and he said, "War has broken out." My brother had two very young children, one four years old and his little girl seven years old, and my mother and I, we were all in the same house. In the yard is my other brother's house, who had a wife, a mother-in-law, and two sons. Around 6.30 or 7.00, somewhere around there, somebody said that in the neighbourhood, [redacted] [redacted]. I went there to see what indeed was going only. He was there. He was tipsy, tipsy, a bit tipsy. I asked him, "Izet, what's going on?" He said that he didn't know, that he didn't know. That's what he said. That's just what he said. Then I asked him where his family was. He said that his people were on the other side. In front of him, he had something like a green rifle. It's the first time I ever saw that kind of thing. I had no idea what it was. And I knew that my brother did not even have a slingshot, this brother who had these very young children. And I took this away from him. I snatched it away from him, from Izet Izetbegovic. And I thought, Well, if this kind of thing is needed, let my brother have it. I left there. And then Pasaga, Pasaga Tihic came up. He is the son-in-law or bother-in-law of Izet Izetbegovic. I got out and went back to my mother's house, and on a small table I left that rifle. My brothers were in the yard. In this same street, only a few houses away, I saw in the street Mr. Franjo Barukcic. That's an elderly gentleman. I ran up to him. Although there was occasional gunfire from the embankment, I saw this Dzeva shooting. I don't know his real name. I just know that nickname of his. He was shooting onto the street. I ran towards Uncle Franjo to ask what was going on. Franjo was frightened, very, very frightened, just like me. I said, "Uncle Franjo, what is this? What's going on? What is this?" Although we had seen war on television, in Croatia and before that in Slovenia, but we were really taken aback. Franjo did not know what to say to me either. He was as frightened as I was. I returned home. Perhaps about half an hour later, I saw a few young men from Samac who wore civilian clothes. They were going up towards the embankment. Among them was Ibrahim Salkic, who on his way back said that he had come to the Prud bridge and that he returned from there. Some of these young men crossed over to Prud, and he returned. That's as far as that day is concerned, I mean, up to noon, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So after you knew that war had broken out, did you return to your own house or did you go back to where your mother and brothers and nephews and nieces were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, no. I was at my mother's house, at my mother's house. I didn't go to my apartment. I didn't dare to, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you stay in your mother's house then for the rest of that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell what was happening outside of the apartment? Did you -- what did you witness from the apartment that was going on outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: You mean that day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day and over the next few days. The first two or three days after war had broken out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon, people started driving round in their cars, different people in different uniforms, quite a few people who I did not even know. Actually, we were watching all of this from the windows. I think that on the next day -- was it the next day or was it that evening? In this other street, away from my mother's house, where this restaurant was where we had been, loud applause was heard. This was late in the afternoon. Something to the effect of the, "Army's coming, the army's coming, the army's coming." You could hear that people were being happy on account of that. Now, I don't know. When this transporter or whatever it is called came to the street where my mother's house is, near the house of some certain Crna, Crna Izet, Izet. His son is Sead Crna. I don't know whether he was in the reserve police or whatever, and he had had some kind of an incident. There was a lot of shooting in front of that house. There was a lot of shooting there. I don't know whether this is a transporter or -- whatever you call it. There was a lot of shooting from that transporter. And several days later, the children brought in these long casings, whatever they are. And then with Stojadin cars -- these were people who were not from Samac, because they spoke Ekavian. They were speaking through a loudspeaker. Is that what you call it? And they were calling this Crna to come out. This was a provocation. He wasn't even there. Opposite them is the house of Dusanka, Sead Ristic, Nezirevic. Somebody moved the curtain, and then they started shooting. And they said, "That's where a sniper shooter is." That was often a pretext. When they entered their -- when they entered our houses, they would say that there was a sniper shooter hiding in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And during these few days when you could see activity of vehicles and some people being detained, did you ever see any of the defendants from your window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: When arms were being collected -- I forgot to say this. That a few hours later on that same day - and thank God that's the way it was - Mr. Izet Izetbegovic came to in front of my mother's house and took that rifle, and he gave me a little pistol, and he left with this. Now, I don't know whether this was two days later or one day later when they were collecting weapons. They were doing all this in a regular sequence. And I saw Mr. Simo Zaric through the window, and Mr. Stojan Blagojevic, that I managed to recognise. They were looking for weapons. My brothers didn't have anything to hand in out of these weapons that were allegedly being distributed. My late brother, my oldest brother, he had a hunting rifle because he was a hunter, and he had legal documents for that. He handed that in to Cvijan Tesic. That was his hunting rifle, and that's what he handed in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Whilst you and your family were in the apartment, were you able to receive information as to what was going on outside? Did you have a radio or other communication from outside your apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, very often when they were cautioning us that we should wear our white armbands, they would be driving round in a car and speaking over a Motorola or whatever you call this thing. They were informing us that we should wear these white armbands when we go out. Secondly, my brother worked at the health centre. He would come back and then we'd hear quite a bit about this from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you were told that "we should wear white armbands." Could you explain to us exactly who was expected to wear white armbands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I don't know who they meant, but while I was going to the SUP to register there, I would see Muslims, Bosniaks, wearing this, and also Catholics, Croats, wearing these white armbands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also explain one other thing to us? You said that the men you had seen around were not from Samac because they spoke Ekavian or with Ekavian accents. Where would that normally mean that they were from? Where was the Ekavian accent from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: This accent is from Serbia proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I think you've told us that you would be informed that you should wear white armbands if you were to go out. Were there other restrictions put on --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other restrictions put on you and others who were living in Bosanski Samac at the time? I'm thinking particularly of the Bosniak and Croat communities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. Soon a curfew was imposed. I don't know whether this is customary when there is a war. Then for a while we were not allowed to lock our houses. And also, we were not supposed to socialise, that three non-Serbs were not allowed to be together. More than three, I mean. More than three were not allowed to be together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever given an explanation as to why you weren't allowed to lock your houses or why more than three non-Serbs shouldn't socialise together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I had no opportunity of asking for an explanation, because very soon I went through this torture of mine. And apart from that, I'm a coward. So I wouldn't dare ask for explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can tell me how long roughly did you stay in the apartment, in your mother's apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: In my mother's apartment, all the time, until I was taken to custody, and later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned now that you were taken to custody, and I'll move on to this incident now. About how long after war had broken out were you, as you said, taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: The eleventh day of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you taken from your mother's apartment then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who came to tell you that you were going to be taken into detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: A police car came with five policemen. I knew one of them personally. We are related. His name is -- his last name is Sejdinovic. Naser is his first name. His nickname is Cagar. And these young men are from our neighbourhood. Rather, they are from the rural area there. I wouldn't know their names, but I know their faces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so how many -- so the five policemen came, and then did they tell you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- what they wanted you for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Sejdinovic said that I was supposed to go in for an interview, to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so did they take you then away to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Three went with me to the MUP and two went up to my mother's house. When we came to the car, one of them pushed me. He pressed my head and pushed me into the car. I was already frightened then. I realised that this would not be just an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take you directly to the MUP or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Directly to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us what happened when you arrived at the MUP? Did you -- were you taken into a room to give your details?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: When I came to the MUP, first I had to report at the reception office where Mr. Djurdjevic was. Was Savo his first name, or whatever? He had come from Croatia. He asked me whether I had shoelaces, a belt, whether I had any of my personal documents on me. He knew me personally, but nevertheless he asked for this, and he wrote this down on a piece of paper, that I had reported in. Then he sent me into the hallway. I stood there in the hallway. Different people were passing by, different people in different uniforms: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military and camouflage uniforms, and police uniforms, and civilian clothes, quite a few of them that I knew as children; for instance, Nesa Lukic, then Savo Savic, et cetera. They passed by, but nobody paid any attention to me until the moment when Mr. Stevan Todorovic came here. And I'm really sorry that he is not here now. I asked him then, "Stevan, Stevo, what am I doing here?" I still could not realise why I was there, what I had done wrong so that I'd have to be at the police station. His answer was, "Madam --" You said that I shouldn't mention my name, right? But he did address me by my name and surname. "You are going to tell us what we don't know." He turned towards Nesa Lukic and said that he should take me upstairs. While we were walking upstairs, -- oh, yes. While I was in the hallway, horrible screams could be heard from the cellar: crying, moans. As we were walking upstairs, as I was walking, a younger man sort of ran by me, a well-built, big young man, and I noticed these tattoos. I'm scared of that, so I noticed that. I remember that. And he was bloodstained all over, and he was playing like this with a truncheon as he was walking upstairs. As you get off the staircase, there is an office, a room, and that's where he took me in. There was a young girl there, and I wanted to sit down, but this girl wouldn't let me sit down. Soon after that, a girl came. Can I mention her name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you can mention her name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, please, you can mention her name if you'd like to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Dilista Prcic came. The door opened and Svetlana Ceca Bozic came in and said we should go to a different room. It's a room that looks out towards Croatia. So that very often they would tell us, "Well, we'll let your own people kill you." But I don't understand what they meant, because they couldn't kill me from Croatia, because I'm a Muslim. So we went to this room. It was like a storage room. It was quite large. There was a shelf right here on this side, and on the shelf were various pieces of uniform; and then on one side there was a chair and in the middle there was a mat, a sort of piece of sponge. I don't know how you would call it. While we were there, we could hear the interrogation from the room next door, shouting: "Where did that Ustasha place the minefields? Where are those minefields?" They wanted him to show where they are. The doors were opening and closing. Young men kept coming in to take a uniform or something else. Each time -- this was still all right before we went through this treatment. Sometimes somebody would say something insulting to us. Not long afterwards the door opened and a gentleman came out. He was wearing camouflage trousers and he was wearing a T-shirt, and he called out, "Dilista Prcic." And he had a lot of trouble reading out her name. He had a lot of trouble reading it out. And he spoke with an Ekavian accent and told her to go to another room. I think that not even ten minutes later, much less than that, you could hear horrible moans, swearing, insults. This was really very loud. It was ringing. And I could really hear it very well in the room where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just before you continue, you've said that people who came into your room used to make insults and that you could hear swearing and insults coming from the other room. What sort of insults and swearing was being directed at you and could you hear from the room next door?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: We were -- and this is still pretty good. I apologise to you. They were cursing our balija mothers, Ustasha mothers, Ustasha whores, whores, sluts, and so on. Samac is a very small town, and everybody knows everybody else very well. I, as a woman, would never be called a slut or a whore by any man in Samac, and I was definitely not one. But from that other room, you could hear insults. Probably they were interrogating a Croat, because you could hear, "Ustasha," cursing his Ustasha mother, "Where are the minefields? Where did you place the minefields?" This is what we could hear. And I say it again: I'm very easily frightened. I get scared very easily. So I was very, very afraid. I didn't know, I couldn't even assume what I would experience in a few minutes -- actually, in about an hour. Dilista stayed there for an hour and then they just brought her back into the room where I was. Then they called me out by my first and last name. My name is also difficult to pronounce, so this man had a lot of trouble with it. When I entered that room -- it was quite a large room and there were about 15 men inside the room. They were all wearing different uniforms and there were different people there. I really didn't recognise any of them at that time. At the table, on the left side, there were a few bottles of a drink called Stock. I noticed that because that drink is packed in very nice bottles, so I noticed them. The table was placed underneath the window and the window was open. It was open wide. I don't know how long it lasted. Out of those 15 men were young enough to be my sons [as interpreted]. They were very young. They didn't even have beards. Five of them were young enough to be my sons. Then a few minutes later ten of them left and then five of them and me stayed in that room. There was a cassette player, and it was on, and you could hear a voice which was congratulating me, wishing me a happy Bajram. Our Bajram was on the 5th of April that year, I think. I was in the office, and a friend of mine, a colleague, came in. His name was Mr. Milos Culapovic. And he literally said this to me, even though I don't know whether this was from my cassette or whether it was taped somewhere, but it was, "Good wishes, sent by Josip Pavelic." And he was my cousin and he was wishing me a happy Bajram. So this was what was playing on that tape, these wishes for a happy Bajram to me. At that moment, a man was standing next to me. I think that nobody in this courtroom is as short as he was. He was very short and he was dark-skinned. On my other side was this gentleman, Lugar. I didn't know, but later I found out from Dilista Prcic that this was Lugar. They ordered me to take my clothes off. At that moment when he told me to take my clothes off, I was shocked. I was surprised. Perhaps this lasted for a moment or perhaps it lasted a little longer, but I just stood there without moving next to that table. And he repeated again, "Take your clothes off, whore." I continued to stand there, and then he slapped me and ordered me to take my clothes off again. I had very narrow-fitting trousers, and I thought that I could gain some time. And I was taking them off very slowly, and I tried to fold them neatly, and I placed them on the table which was on my left-hand side. Unluckily for me, at that time, I had my period. So then I also had to take off my underpants, and I did take them off, and I tried to, to arrange or fold it in such a way so that they wouldn't see my sanitary napkin. At that moment, one of them swore, and he said, "You dirty balija," something like that. And it was very insulting. And he took my clothes and threw them in the direction of the door. And he told me to lie down on the table, to spread my legs. It was a desk, a work desk, and it had drawers on the sides. I simply couldn't understand that something like this could ever happen to me in my life, that I would have to lie down on a table in front of five men. At the time that he was ordering me to do this and pushing me towards the desk, this young man, this short man, took out -- I don't know whether he took out a knife from his boot or from his pants. And he stood next to the table and told me to lie in such a way that this knife was resting right underneath my throat and that I couldn't, mustn't move, that I had to stay still. Somebody who was standing behind my back said, "Fifty strokes with a belt," and 50 -- he didn't say a bat, but he used - I don't know - some other term. I don't know which one. But they did hit me with a bat. He didn't say the word "bat." He said something else. The whole time that they were beating me, they were insulting me so terribly that even if I had five more lives, I don't think that I could hear such insults again. It's true that each -- the first time that they hit me, the knife fell. That's true. It flipped over. I was crying. Then they turned up the music so loudly. You could hear this music throbbing above your head. They were insulting me and hitting me. A couple of times I felt really, really weak. I felt sick. And then one of them said that they should cool me off, and he urinated on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you okay? Would you like to take a glass -- do you want to take a sip of water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I'm fine. At one moment, I felt sick, and I probably slipped off the table so that as I slipped or I don't know if they turned me, but I was facing the door. At that moment, I saw Mr. Zaric standing at the door. And as Mr. Zaric was standing, a gentleman passed by him who addressed one of these men. He cursed God, and he said, "What are you doing to this woman?" The man was speaking in an Ekavian accent. He was from Serbia proper. And I noticed that as he raised his hand towards this other man, I noticed that he didn't have -- some of his fingers were missing. Mr. Zaric left. I don't know if he did anything or not, but they continued to beat me, probably to -- to strike me 50 blows, which was what they were planning to do. Afterwards, two soldiers pulled me out, dragged me out of this room and took me to the other room, and they laid me down on this mat. Yes. Do you understand what I mean when I say "mat"? This piece of sponge. And this gentleman, Laki, was there again. That's what they said later that his name was. And I would like to thank him a hundred times. He went to get my clothes. While those two soldiers were taking me out, my -- they were taking inside the room my neighbour Barukcic, and across from there I could see Bicic -- no, not Bicic, Dzemal Muric, called Dzemak. Since I had my period, and I had received so many blows and this man had urinated on me as well, I was also covered with blood. And this man, Laki - I don't know his proper name - went to get my clothes, and together with Dilista, they dressed me. I was not feeling very well again. I felt faint. This woman, Dilista, she was a very brave woman. She asked Svetlana Ceca Bozic for a glass of water. However, she didn't permit her to get this glass of water. She said we were prisoners and she could not give us a glass of water. Again this gentleman went out and he brought us water, and then he said, "Madam" -- he didn't know my name. He was asking, "Madam, what did you do so that they are doing this to you?" I don't know what I did. I didn't know to this day what I did. And I'm here mostly in order that somebody here would tell me now what is it that I did wrong so that this happened to me. He went to get us water. The water was in a jar. He said that he had never hit a woman. By "hitting," he probably meant in the way that we were hit. But he said that if we did anything to ourselves, that he would not help us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask you is to pause there for a minute? And I'd just like to ask you some questions about what you've told us. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the room, you said that you were getting a lot of insults and insults like you'd never heard. Were they the same sort of insults that you had been receiving when you were waiting to be taken into the room where the table was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: While we were waiting, what we were going through was nothing compared to the insults that you could hear around. It was really something that a normal mind cannot even comprehend. I think really that those people were not normal. Each one of them has a mother. They have a sister. How could they not imagine their mother or their sister perhaps in our place? I don't know. Yes. And I forgot to say while they were hitting me, they kept telling me the whole time that I was cursing their Serbian or Chetnik mother, which is quite impossible, really impossible. This was the beginning of the war. In my ears, in my vocabulary, the word "Chetnik" was something that was really not familiar to me. There was no way I could have cursed somebody's Chetnik mother. They kept saying that I cursed their Serbian, their Chetnik mother. And then they were cursing me, my balija mother and my Ustasha mother. They used all kinds of insults and curses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You indicated that at one stage after you had fallen from the table, you looked up to see Simo Zaric at the doorway. Was he in the hallway or the doorway or was he actually in where --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: He was inside the door of the room. So he was inside the room, inside the doorway. That's where Mr. Zaric was standing. I don't know for how long he could have been standing there, because I had my back to the door and they were hitting me for a long time and I was feeling faint. So I just saw him for an instant. But I know that at that moment, since at that time, and now I respect Mr. Zaric very much, I was very much ashamed that he could see me in such -- in such a state. I was bloody. I was naked. It was really, really, ugly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the person who came in beside Mr. Zaric, Mr. Laki, had said, "What are you doing to this woman?" Did Mr. Zaric ever try to intervene or say anything to the men who were hitting you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, not Mr. Zaric. Yes. Yes. I don't know. Mr. Zaric left, so I don't know whether he intervened somewhere or not, but he didn't intervene while I was in the room. At least I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember at the time what Mr. Zaric was wearing? Was he in civilian clothes, military clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: When I used to see Mr. Zaric during the war, I would see him in a camouflage uniform, especially at the beginning of the war. I would see him quite often, because I had to report every morning and every evening. I had to report to the MUP or the SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think the question was answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me specifically at that time when you saw at the doorway, at the doorway, so not other times that you saw him but when you saw him there in the doorway, can you remember what clothes he was in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I really am not able to remember now because I was in such a state that -- really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you were eventually taken out of that room and you were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. In the late afternoon, I would meet Mr. Zaric again at the exit to the MUP, and I saw him then. At that time, he was wearing a camouflage uniform. But at that moment, I'm under oath, and I really am not able to tell you what he was wearing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you were taken to -- when you were eventually taken out of the room where the beating occurred, you were placed in a room where Dilista was and that you were helped to dress and given a glass of water. Can you explain to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, not then. This gentleman helped me, and Dilista. Yes, two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber how you felt then at that time in the room after you'd gone through this beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There are many women here right now. I don't know if even for a minute you can imagine how a woman feels in a situation where you are completely helpless and you are surrounded by drunken, drugged, and rude people who are humiliating you so much. I felt very, very miserable, really miserable and hurt and humiliated.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's coming up to 11.00. I'm going to ask about what happened during the rest of that stay, and rather than go into a detailed discussion, maybe we should make a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can have our break and continue our proceedings at 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Welcome back. When we took our break, you were just telling us how you had felt after you had been returned to the room where you were with Dilista now and you had been -- you had your clothes back on and you had been given a glass of water. How much longer did you stay in that room for that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: All the time up to the curfew we stayed in that room. Soon after that -- actually, Dilista went out into the hallway, because there was a man called Cedo Simic there who had gone to school with her, and she came back from the hall and she said that Cedo had said to her that they were getting some people ready to go to Brcko, and maybe we would go to Brcko too, she said. Soon after that they came to get Dilista, and she went to the room where she had gone from. She didn't stay long. She came back. She said that she had been questioned by Mr. Dragan Djordjevic and Mr. Simo Zaric, that they were very correct, that they only showed her some lists on which the name of her relative, Sefko Prcic [phoen] was, and they asked her about him. So she returned very soon, as I said. I don't know how much time had gone by. Mr. Stevan Todorovic walked in. Since I could not sit, I was sort of kneeling on that mat. I was leaning on my hands and knees. He passed behind my back and he kicked me in the rear. He looked at me and then he slapped me in the face. And he asked me whether my nose could pierce the sky now, and he said to me -- he addressed me by my name, my first name. He said, "You know, this was not done to you by the Serbs; this was done to you by your own people." That's the way he had put it. And then he left. After --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a question before you continue? You said that Dilista had left the room, and when she came back, she told you that she had been interrogated by a man called Dragan Djordjevic and Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I correct that this interrogation had taken place after Dilista had received her beatings of 80 lashes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you also tell me: You said that you couldn't sit and therefore you were kneeling.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this because you had --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- wounds on your back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: It wasn't wounds. Only two days later -- actually, that evening when I arrived - I thought that I would tell you about this later - there was a doctor there, Mesud Nogic, Dr. Mesud Nogic, and Dr. Ruza Brdar Masic, and they examined me. I wanted to tell you about that later, but do you want me to tell you about it now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can tell us about that later when we get to that. I just wanted to clarify: Was the reason you couldn't sit, was that a direct result of the beatings that you had received in the other room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I had been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So my understanding is correct, is it, that the reason that you had to kneel down was because you were still so sore on your back from the beatings that the men had given you in the other room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Can I answer your question now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: The strokes went on for a long time, or rather, I felt their effects for about ten days, at least, that entire part of my body that they had been beating, here above the kidneys. And then the strokes went down all the way to the knees. On the one side this man with the belt was beating me, and on the other side, this man with a bat. So it was like when you're putting cubes one on to another. The strokes just followed one after the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Ms. Reidy, perhaps to clarify if I could ask the

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: had wanted to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: The room where you say you were kneeling down and then Mr. Todorovic, you say, kicked you. I'm asking you whether you had to kneel because there was nowhere where you could sit, a chair, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a bench, and we could not sit there, no way. Dilista was kneeling on her knees and was leaning with her hands against this bench. When they threw me in, they threw me onto that mat immediately, that sponge mat. And then when they dressed me, Dilista and Mr. Laki, I remained in that same position, because that's the only position I could sustain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question on that. Was it painful for you to try to move into any other position then?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Although while it was still warm, so to speak, it was sort of all right. The real pain came later when it all cooled off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you. Now, you've told us that Mr. Todorovic came in and that he kicked you.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Dilista had heard some information that you may be transferred to Brcko with some male prisoners. Were you taken to Brcko with the male prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think maybe you didn't answer me. So were you and Dilista actually taken to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you know why you weren't taken to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Since people were coming in and out of that room all the time, the door was open. And at one moment a voice was heard, a voice that was saying precisely this: "If you take," and then they mentioned the name, "then take me as well." Mr. Milorad Aleksic, nicknamed Miso came up to the door. Since the door was ajar, I said, "Miso." I called out to him. However, Miso waved his hand and left. And I thought, my goodness, now even Miso won't help. He went across the hall. After awhile, it was getting dark and that's probably when the curfew was coming up. I don't know whether it was at 7.00 or 8.00. I don't know when the curfew actually started. They came to pick me up, and they said that I was going to see Stevan Todorovic. I came to him. He was sitting at a desk, and there was also a small table there by the side, and there was a man sitting there, Mr. Radovic. Mladen was his first name. He didn't even raise his head. He was probably ashamed to see me there. At least that's the way I take it. Stevan said that we should go home and that from the next day onwards, we should report in the morning at 7.00 and in the evening at 7.00 every day. He opened the door, and again he shouted out, he called out the name of this young man, Nesa Lukic. He said that he should drive us, that he should take us in the car. However, Dilista had come with her car. I always say of this woman that she is very brave, exceptionally brave. And she said that a driver did not have to take us, that she would take us. When we came to the car, she opened the door. I couldn't sit down. She had a Renault 4. I was in the back seat, and I was leaning forward, and she said literally, "Now you're going to see how you can sit on the back." Somehow she managed to drive us home, only God knows. The next day she walked, because there was no way she could sit in the car again when we went in the morning to report again. Oh, I'm sorry. As we were getting out of the MUP, at the very door, I met Mr. Simo Zaric, Mr. Savo Cancarevic, and Mr. Radovan Antic. They were getting in. I said at the outset as well that I take Mr. Zaric to be a friend, and that's how I took him then as well. It's a very narrow hallway, and I leaned against him, and Mr. Zaric said to me that I should never say anywhere what I had experienced and why I was beaten up, because I have three brothers. My understanding then was a threat, that that was a threat. I don't know which way Mr. Zaric meant it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I go back now and ask you some questions about the next -- that portion of your testimony? You mentioned that when you were still up in the room, you'd heard a person with the surname Aleksic, nicknamed Miso, you said.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what function Miso had in the MUP or in the military?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was in the MUP, but Miso was a soldier of the Republika Srpska. At that time, the daughter of my late friend Dzuheric Enes, his daughter Melita Dzuheric came around 12.00 to my mother's home, and my mother said that we -- that they had taken me to the MUP. Melita took her bike to the Savski Most, the bridge on the Sava River, and she found Miso there. Miso is her uncle. And she said to him that they took me to the MUP. By profession, Miso is a land surveyor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said he was a member of the Republika Srpska, I think you said, a soldier of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what he did as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: At that time, they were laying mines by the bridge on the Sava so that the other army would not cross the bridge coming from the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you talk of "the other side," what do you mean, Witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My town is divided only by the Sava River. Croatia is on the other side. And they were probably afraid that this Croatian army might cross the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this Miso, again you said that you heard him say that -- something like, "If you take her with me -- if you take her to Brcko, you must take me too."

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was quarreling with someone in the hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who he was quarreling with? Could you see that from your room?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But after you heard him quarreling, do I understand that you weren't taken to Brcko then?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No, we were not taken to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I also understand from your testimony that you yourself were never interrogated that day or didn't have to give a statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, nobody asked me a thing. I was beaten up, insulted, and I never gave any statement to anyone. I have never known what I'm being blamed for and what it is that I had done wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us that on the way out, you had passed by three persons, I think it's Savo Cancarevic, Radovan Antic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, were all three men wearing military uniform?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric and Mr. Cancarevic were. As for Mr. Antic, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell whether Mr. Zaric was carrying a weapon or whether he was unarmed?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said he also said to you not to say ever what had happened to you because that you had three brothers?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you took that as a threat.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: That's how I took it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- did you take the threat seriously? Were you frightened by what he had said?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Very seriously. I expected Mr. Zaric to react differently. As I said, we were friends. I like Mr. Zaric. I appreciate him. I respect him. And I expected him to react quite differently, because had the situation - heaven forbid - been the other way around, I as a woman certainly would have reacted differently had it been Simo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that the only thing that passed between you, this threat? He didn't say anything else to you?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No. No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't say anything back to him after he'd threatened you?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that Dilista then drove you to your house or your mother's house?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: My mother's house. At my house there were already other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber what you mean when you say that at your house there were already other people?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: They had broken into the house. [redacted] [phoen], and her husband. They stayed there for about two months. They only changed the lock on the door. They didn't move a thing. Everything was the way I had left it. They really didn't touch a thing. Once I had the opportunity of meeting [redacted]. She is from Slavonski Samac. I thought she was a Catholic, so I said to her, [redacted] [redacted] [phoen], you a Catholic, me a Muslim. Why did you enter my house?" And as I said to you, they were there for two months, that is, from the moment when they broke into the house, and then two months later the keys were returned to me. They didn't touch a thing. The keys were returned to me. But soon, three or four days later, perhaps, Mr. [redacted] came, who worked in the same company with me. He said to me that I should give him the keys to my apartment of my own free will or that he would come with armed people and throw me out so that he could move into my house. He allowed me to take out the furniture from my living room, and some other things, and then the police came. I think -- actually, it's not that I think. I'm sure that he called the police. And they asked me, where is my warrant, do I have a warrant for taking my things out of my house? And I said that I did not have a warrant, because I was terribly afraid of the police. Since I had experienced what I had experienced, I would have left everything for them there and gone away. However, I did take this part of my things and I left this with [redacted] [phoen], a neighbour of mine, and I left it for safekeeping with him, but I never got it back, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This person [redacted] [phoen], who you've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll call him Dragan. Do you know what ethnic background he had?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: A Serb, a Serb, Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you finally find out whether Mandric Bozic -- which ethnic background she had?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: She was Orthodox. There are a few houses that are Orthodox in Slavonski Samac, and she was from one of them. Although I said that these people had really not touched a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you didn't get the things back you had left for safekeeping. Did you -- were you ever given any official document from the police who came, or from this [redacted], that showed that he was entitled to have your house or take over your apartment?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you: I was not evicted by the official authorities who were then evicting non-Serbs from their homes. I was evicted by [redacted]. He did not have any documents. He didn't show me anything. He just threatened me. And due to his threat, I left. He said to me, since he painted my apartment -- on the 11th of January is the anniversary of the death of my late husband, and I always commemorate that day. This [redacted] was painting my house in January, and then he said to me, when he was evicting me from the apartment, that on the 11th of January he knew that that would be his apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the police had come, though, whilst you were trying to gather some of your possessions. Did they try to stop Dragan evicting you from your apartment?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No. They prevented me from taking my things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also told me that there were the Serb -- I think the Serb authorities who were evicting non-Serbs from their apartments. How did you find out about this information?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: My daughter-in-law was thrown out like that. She was in the same yard together with me. Some people came. [redacted] [phoen] [redacted]. I think her last name was Petkovic. And they told them that they have to leave their homes. They wrote down -- made a list of all their belongings and told them that they had to leave, and this happened to other people in my neighbourhood. They drove them out to Zasavica and further out. Across the street from my mother's house there's a [redacted]family living there, and at that time I saw a barefoot woman, an elderly woman in her 60s, and her husband as well. She was placed in a truck with no shoes and in bare feet, and her husband too, and they were taken to Zasavica like that. I happened to see that, because my movements were restricted, so that I don't know too much about what was happening further out, but I was able to see what was going on in my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And these people who were moved to Zasavica, for example, the elderly woman and the man, were they ever told why they had to leave their houses and why they were being put on trucks and forced into Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Let me tell you: I don't know what they were told, because I didn't talk to them. Those people went to Zasavica. But I know about my sister-in-law, because this happened in our yard. My sister-in-law was still there, and they told her that they were going to take her to Zasavica the next day. And somebody moved in to her first floor, and she spent that night in her -- on the ground floor of her place, and that night she was there, but then the next day she went to Zasavica and then further on. There were six families in one kitchen [as interpreted] In Zasavica. There was my mother; myself; my mother's sister; my brother's mother-in-law, also who was expelled; my aunt, who had been expelled from her house; my cousin. There were five of us, five families who had all been expelled from our homes. [redacted] [redacted]. These were all families who were expelled from our homes. They were not expelled by anybody in authority, while I was expelled by Dragan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to clarify one or two things? I don't understand, and it may be a problem just with the transcript which I see in front of me. You said that there were -- the transcript says that you said there were six families in one kitchen in Zasavica. Do you mean there were six families --

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you then tell us -- [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No. No. No. I didn't say "in Zasavica." [redacted] [redacted]."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say that your mother, yourself, your mother's sister, your brother's mother-in-law, and your aunt and your cousin were all together in one family -- in one kitchen, you mean they were all evicted from their houses [redacted]? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I didn't say "kitchen." I said "in [redacted] [redacted] house."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And then the other thing I'd just like to clarify is: You said that while you were expelled by [redacted], they were not expelled by anyone in authority. Do you mean that they were expelled by someone in authority or that they were not expelled by someone in authority?

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: No. I was not expelled by anybody in power. I was expelled by [redacted], while all the others were expelled -- my mother's sister is an old woman in her 70s. She is 77 or 78. She was that age at the time. She wasn't able to go to Zasavica. She had a broken hip, so she was staying at my mother's house. Dika Cehajic, she is also an elderly woman of 62, 63 at that time. She was expelled from her flat. She was in Zasavica, and then from Zasavica, through some connection of hers, she was released. So she was also staying at my mother's house. She was with us. Risaha Jusufovic, he was expelled. He was expelled by the authorities. He received a warrant to leave, an order to leave his house. He was living in my mother's house, and I was also living in my mother's house, and of course my mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, I think I understand your living situation at that moment in terms of where you were staying and why you couldn't return to your own apartment. Could you please now tell us what happened after you arrived home that first evening from the SUP after Dilista had brought you back in her car.

utterances.speaker: Was there a chair in that room that you could have sat on if you
utterances.text: Before I came back home, my mother knew more or less what happened to me, because [redacted], my neighbour, my mother's first neighbour, was passing by. He had been at the SUP and then he heard from some young people who were downstairs at the building that two mature women were beaten up, and he knew before that that we had been taken in. So that even -- so when I got home, my mother didn't even ask anything. She was crying, and of course I was crying together with her. Shortly afterwards, Dr. Mesud Nogic came by. He examined me a little bit. He lifted up my top, and he looked. He also took down my lower clothes to see how I was. And then he said he was going to the health centre, to the medical centre, and that he would send something for me so that I could make dressings and place them on my back. I think it was Rivanol or something like that.
